title: Accelerating a Strong-Coupling Non-Equilibrium Steady-State Impurity Solver using (Quantics) Tensor Trains
abstract: Including higher order diagrammatic corrections to the strong-coupling expansion is mainly limited by the evaluation of high-dimensional, time-ordered integrals. In this work we present and compare four different parametrizations of the integrands in order to obtain a low-rank (quantics) tensor-train representation using tensor cross interpolation. Particular emphasis is placed on a quantics time-difference formulation in which the required retarded convolutions are performed directly in quantics tensor-train form. Using controlled Gaussian benchmarks, we analyze the accuracy, bond dimensions, and computational scaling of the different approaches. We then validate the most promising formulations in self-consistent equilibrium and nonequilibrium DMFT calculations and demonstrate calculations up to the third order in the strong-coupling expansion. Finally, we extend the solver to impurity models with retarded density-density interactions and apply it within nonequilibrium extended DMFT. Our results show that tensor cross interpolation substantially reduces the cost of evaluating higher-order diagrams and provides a controlled, systematically improvable framework for nonequilibrium quantum impurity calculations.
summary: This paper introduces an advanced computational technique combining Tensor Cross Interpolation and Quantics Tensor-Trains to efficiently calculate high-dimensional integrals arising in the strong-coupling expansion of quantum impurity models. By implementing this method directly into the real-time Keldysh formalism, the authors achieve a controlled and scalable solver for non-equilibrium steady states in correlated electron systems.
main_problem: The primary challenge is evaluating high-dimensional, time-ordered integrals arising from the strong-coupling expansion for quantum impurity models in non-equilibrium steady states (NESS).
main_result: The combination of Tensor Cross Interpolation and Quantics Tensor-Train representations substantially reduces the computational cost of evaluating higher-order diagrams, enabling systematic calculations up to the third order.
method: The authors employ a strong-coupling expansion within the Keldysh formalism, utilizing Tensor Cross Interpolation (TCI) to decompose high-dimensional tensors into a low-rank Quantics Tensor-Train (QTT) format for efficient computation of retarded convolutions.
model_or_system: The work focuses on quantum impurity models, specifically addressing non-equilibrium steady states using the Anderson model and extended Dynamical Mean Field Theory (DMFT) with retarded density-density interactions. The formalism is built around solving Dyson equations for pseudo-particle propagators.
key_observables: Pseudo-particle propagator $\hat{G}(t, t')$, self-energy $\hat{\Sigma}(t, t')$, and physical correlation functions $C_{AB}(t, t')$.
important_parameters: The order of the strong-coupling expansion (up to third order), bond dimensions ($\chi$), and artificial broadening parameter ($\eta$).
main_assumptions: The method assumes that transient dynamics decay sufficiently fast to allow for a NESS description, necessitating an artificial damping factor $\eta$ in calculations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the Keldysh contour structure, examples of self-energy diagrams (OCA), and show convergence tests for spectral functions (NCA, OCA, TOA) as a function of broadening ($\eta$) or bond dimension ($\chi$).
paper_structure: The paper develops the formalism by first establishing the need to evaluate high-dimensional integrals in NESS. It then introduces TCI/QTT for tensor decomposition and applies this machinery to solve the Dyson equation iteratively, culminating in calculations of higher-order self-energies.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, systematically improvable numerical framework for calculating non-equilibrium quantum dynamics in strongly correlated systems, which is crucial for understanding open quantum systems far from equilibrium.
